content.text:
I now have all the information needed. Here is my research summary.

## Research Summary: Claude Code Plugin Specification

### 1. Plugin Directory Layout (Required Structure)

```
my-plugin/
├── .claude-plugin/
│   └── plugin.json           # Manifest (optional but recommended)
├── skills/                   # Skills as <name>/SKILL.md directories
│   └── my-skill/
│       ├── SKILL.md          # Required per skill
│       ├── reference.md      # Optional supporting files
│       └── scripts/          # Optional scripts
├── commands/                 # Legacy: flat .md skill files (use skills/ instead)
├── agents/                   # Subagent definition .md files
├── hooks/
│   └── hooks.json            # Hook event handlers
├── output-styles/            # Output style definitions
├── bin/                      # Executables added to Bash tool's PATH
├── scripts/                  # Hook and utility scripts
├── settings.json             # Default settings (only "agent" key supported)
├── .mcp.json                 # MCP server configurations
├── .lsp.json                 # LSP server configurations
├── LICENSE
└── CHANGELOG.md
```

**Critical rule**: Only `plugin.json` goes inside `.claude-plugin/`. All other directories (skills/, commands/, agents/, hooks/, etc.) must be at the plugin root.

### 2. plugin.json -- Complete Schema

**Required fields** (if manifest is included): Only `name` is required.

```json
{
  "name": "plugin-name",
  "version": "1.2.0",
  "description": "Brief plugin description",
  "author": {
    "name": "Author Name",
    "email": "author@example.com",
    "url": "https://github.com/author"
  },
  "homepage": "https://docs.example.com/plugin",
  "repository": "https://github.com/author/plugin",
  "license": "MIT",
  "keywords": ["keyword1", "keyword2"],
  "skills": "./custom/skills/",
  "commands": ["./custom/commands/special.md"],
  "agents": "./custom/agents/",
  "hooks": "./config/hooks.json",
  "mcpServers": "./mcp-config.json",
  "outputStyles": "./styles/",
  "lspServers": "./.lsp.json",
  "userConfig": {
    "api_endpoint": {
      "description": "Your team's API endpoint",
      "sensitive": false
    },
    "api_token": {
      "description": "API authentication token",
      "sensitive": true
    }
  },
  "channels": [
    {
      "server": "telegram",
      "userConfig": {
        "bot_token": { "description": "Telegram bot token", "sensitive": true }
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

**Field details**:

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
|-------|------|----------|-------------|
| `name` | string | Yes (if manifest exists) | Kebab-case, no spaces. Used as namespace prefix for skills. |
| `version` | string | No | Semver. If also in marketplace entry, plugin.json wins. |
| `description` | string | No | Brief explanation |
| `author` | object | No | `name` (string), `email` (string), `url` (string) |
| `homepage` | string | No | Documentation URL |
| `repository` | string | No | Source code URL |
| `license` | string | No | SPDX identifier |
| `keywords` | array | No | Discovery tags |
| `skills` | string or array | No | Custom skill paths (replaces default `skills/`) |
| `commands` | string or array | No | Custom command paths (replaces default `commands/`) |
| `agents` | string or array | No | Custom agent paths (replaces default `agents/`) |
| `hooks` | string, array, or object | No | Hook config paths or inline config |
| `mcpServers` | string, array, or object | No | MCP config paths or inline config |
| `outputStyles` | string or array | No | Custom output style paths |
| `lspServers` | string, array, or object | No | LSP server configs |
| `userConfig` | object | No | User-configurable values prompted at enable time |
| `channels` | array | No | Channel declarations for message injection |

**Path behavior**: All paths must be relative and start with `./`. Custom paths for skills/commands/agents/outputStyles **replace** the default directory. To keep both, include the default in an array: `"skills": ["./skills/", "./extras/"]`.

**The manifest is optional**. If omitted, Claude Code auto-discovers components in default locations and derives the plugin name from the directory name.

### 3. hooks.json Format

Located at `hooks/hooks.json` in the plugin root.

```json
{
  "description": "Optional description of hooks",
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Write|Edit",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/format-code.sh",
            "timeout": 30,
            "async": false,
            "statusMessage": "Formatting..."
          }
        ]
      }
    ],
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Bash",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/security-check.sh"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

**All supported event types**: `SessionStart`, `SessionEnd`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `PostToolUseFailure`, `PermissionRequest`, `PermissionDenied`, `Stop`, `StopFailure`, `SubagentStart`, `SubagentStop`, `TaskCreated`, `TaskCompleted`, `TeammateIdle`, `InstructionsLoaded`, `ConfigChange`, `CwdChanged`, `FileChanged`, `WorktreeCreate`, `WorktreeRemove`, `PreCompact`, `PostCompact`, `Elicitation`, `ElicitationResult`, `Notification`

**Hook handler types**:
- `command`: Shell command execution. Fields: `command` (required), `async`, `shell`, `timeout`, `if`, `statusMessage`, `once`
- `http`: POST to a URL. Fields: `url` (required), `headers`, `allowedEnvVars`, `timeout`
- `prompt`: LLM evaluation. Fields: `prompt` (required), `model`, `timeout`
- `agent`: Agentic verifier with tools. Fields: `prompt` (required), `timeout`

**Matcher syntax**: Omitted or `"*"` matches all. Pipe-separated strings for exact match (e.g., `"Write|Edit"`). Other patterns treated as JavaScript regex.

**Environment variables available**: `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` (plugin install dir) and `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}` (persistent data dir).

### 4. Agent Definition Files

Located in `agents/` directory. Each agent is a Markdown file with YAML frontmatter.

```markdown
---
name: security-reviewer
description: Reviews code for security vulnerabilities. Use when analyzing code for security issues.
model: sonnet
effort: medium
maxTurns: 20
disallowedTools: Write, Edit
---

You are a security expert. When invoked, analyze code for:
1. SQL injection vulnerabilities
2. XSS attack vectors
3. Authentication bypasses
4. Insecure data handling
```

**Supported frontmatter fields for plugin agents**:

| Field | Required | Description |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| `name` | Yes | Unique identifier, lowercase with hyphens |
| `description` | Yes | When Claude should delegate to this agent |
| `model` | No | `sonnet`, `opus`, `haiku`, full model ID, or `inherit` |
| `effort` | No | `low`, `medium`, `high`, `max` |
| `maxTurns` | No | Maximum agentic turns |
| `tools` | No | Allowlist of tools |
| `disallowedTools` | No | Tools to deny |
| `skills` | No | Skills to preload at startup |
| `memory` | No | `user`, `project`, or `local` |
| `background` | No | `true` to always run as background task |
| `isolation` | No | Only valid value: `"worktree"` |
| `color` | No | Display color: red/blue/green/yellow/purple/orange/pink/cyan |

**Security restriction for plugin agents**: `hooks`, `mcpServers`, and `permissionMode` fields are **NOT supported** in plugin-shipped agents and are silently ignored.

### 5. marketplace.json Specification

Located at `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` in the marketplace repository root.

```json
{
  "name": "company-tools",
  "owner": {
    "name": "DevTools Team",
    "email": "devtools@example.com"
  },
  "metadata": {
    "description": "Company development tools",
    "version": "1.0.0",
    "pluginRoot": "./plugins"
  },
  "plugins": [
    {
      "name": "code-formatter",
      "source": "./plugins/formatter",
      "description": "Automatic code formatting on save",
      "version": "2.1.0",
      "author": { "name": "DevTools Team" },
      "category": "formatting",
      "tags": ["lint", "format"],
      "keywords": ["formatting", "prettier"],
      "homepage": "https://docs.example.com",
      "repository": "https://github.com/company/formatter",
      "license": "MIT",
      "strict": true
    },
    {
      "name": "deploy-tools",
      "source": {
        "source": "github",
        "repo": "company/deploy-plugin",
        "ref": "v2.0.0",
        "sha": "a1b2c3d4e5f6..."
      },
      "description": "Deployment automation"
    }
  ]
}
```

**Required marketplace fields**:

| Field | Type | Description |
|-------|------|-------------|
| `name` | string | Kebab-case identifier. Users see this in install commands. |
| `owner` | object | `name` (required string), `email` (optional string) |
| `plugins` | array | List of plugin entries |

**Reserved marketplace names** (cannot be used): `claude-code-marketplace`, `claude-code-plugins`, `claude-plugins-official`, `anthropic-marketplace`, `anthropic-plugins`, `agent-skills`, `knowledge-work-plugins`, `life-sciences`. Names impersonating official marketplaces are also blocked.

**Optional metadata**: `metadata.description`, `metadata.version`, `metadata.pluginRoot` (base directory prepended to relative source paths).

**Plugin entry required fields**: `name` (string) and `source` (string or object).

**Plugin source types**:
- **Relative path**: `"./plugins/my-plugin"` (string starting with `./`)
- **GitHub**: `{ "source": "github", "repo": "owner/repo", "ref": "v2.0", "sha": "abc123..." }`
- **Git URL**: `{ "source": "url", "url": "https://...", "ref": "...", "sha": "..." }`
- **Git subdirectory**: `{ "source": "git-subdir", "url": "...", "path": "...", "ref": "...", "sha": "..." }`
- **npm**: `{ "source": "npm", "package": "@company/plugin", "version": "^1.0.0", "registry": "..." }`

**Plugin entry optional fields**: `description`, `version`, `author`, `homepage`, `repository`, `license`, `keywords`, `category`, `tags`, `strict` (boolean, default true), plus all component configuration fields from plugin.json (`skills`, `commands`, `agents`, `hooks`, `mcpServers`, `lspServers`).

### 6. SKILL.md Format Within Plugins

```yaml
---
name: code-review
description: Reviews code for best practices. Use when reviewing code, checking PRs.
argument-hint: "[filename] [format]"
disable-model-invocation: false
user-invocable: true
allowed-tools: Read Grep Glob
model: sonnet
effort: medium
context: fork
agent: Explore
paths: "**/*.ts, **/*.js"
shell: bash
hooks:
  PreToolUse:
    - matcher: "Bash"
      hooks:
        - type: command
          command: "./scripts/check.sh"
---

Skill instructions in markdown here...
```

**All frontmatter fields**: `name`, `description`, `argument-hint`, `disable-model-invocation`, `user-invocable`, `allowed-tools`, `model`, `effort`, `context`, `agent`, `hooks`, `paths`, `shell`.

**String substitutions**: `$ARGUMENTS`, `$ARGUMENTS[N]` / `$N`, `${CLAUDE_SESSION_ID}`, `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}`.

**Dynamic context injection**: `` !`command` `` syntax runs shell commands before skill content is sent to Claude. Multi-line via ` ```! ` fenced blocks.

### 7. Approval Criteria and Publishing

**Official marketplace submission**: Use the in-app submission forms:
- Claude.ai: `claude.ai/settings/plugins/submit`
- Console: `platform.claude.com/plugins/submit`

**Official repository**: `github.com/anthropics/claude-plugins-official` has two directories:
- `/plugins` -- Internal Anthropic-developed plugins
- `/external_plugins` -- Third-party partner plugins

**Known approval criteria**:
- Must meet quality standards (not fully public criteria)
- Must meet security standards
- Subject to Anthropic review and approval
- Plugins with "Anthropic Verified" badge have undergone additional quality and safety review
- There is a basic automated review before being added to the directory
- External plugins submitted via the plugin directory submission form

**Important caveat from Anthropic**: "Make sure you trust a plugin before installing, updating, or using it. Anthropic does not control what MCP servers, files, or other software are included in plugins and cannot verify that they will work as intended or that they won't change."

**Self-hosted marketplace distribution** (no approval needed): Push your marketplace repo to GitHub/GitLab, users add it with `/plugin marketplace add owner/repo`.

### 8. Key Validation Points for Your Repo

Things to check against your existing skills structure at `/Users/pepe/Library/CloudStorage/OneDrive-TV2DANMARK/Dokumenter/GitHub/pskoett-skills`:

1. Your repo currently uses the Agent Skills open standard (`skills/*/SKILL.md` with YAML frontmatter). This is compatible with the Claude Code plugin format.
2. To become a proper plugin, you need `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` at the repo root.
3. To become a marketplace, you need `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`.
4. Skills need to be in `skills/` at the plugin root (which matches your current layout).
5. Plugin `name` in plugin.json must be kebab-case with no spaces.
6. SKILL.md frontmatter should have at least `name` and `description`.
7. For official marketplace submission, use `claude.ai/settings/plugins/submit` or `platform.claude.com/plugins/submit`.

### Sources Consulted

- [Create plugins - Claude Code Docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins) -- Official plugin creation guide
- [Plugins reference - Claude Code Docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins-reference) -- Complete technical specification

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
|-------|------|----------|-------------|
| `name` | string | Yes (if manifest exists) | Kebab-case, no spaces. Used as namespace prefix for skills. |
| `version` | string | No | Semver. If also in marketplace entry, plugin.json wins. |
| `description` | string | No | Brief explanation |
| `author` | object | No | `name` (string), `email` (string), `url` (string) |
| `homepage` | string | No | Documentation URL |
| `repository` | string | No | Source code URL |
| `license` | string | No | SPDX identifier |
| `keywords` | array | No | Discovery tags |
| `skills` | string or array | No | Custom skill paths (replaces default `skills/`) |
| `commands` | string or array | No | Custom command paths (replaces default `commands/`) |
| `agents` | string or array | No | Custom agent paths (replaces default `agents/`) |
| `hooks` | string, array, or object | No | Hook config paths or inline config |
| `mcpServers` | string, array, or object | No | MCP config paths or inline config |
| `outputStyles` | string or array | No | Custom output style paths |
| `lspServers` | string, array, or object | No | LSP server configs |
| `userConfig` | object | No | User-configurable values prompted at enable time |
| `channels` | array | No | Channel declarations for message injection |

**Path behavior**: All paths must be relative and start with `./`. Custom paths for skills/commands/agents/outputStyles **replace** the default directory. To keep both, include the default in an array: `"skills": ["./skills/", "./extras/"]`.

**The manifest is optional**. If omitted, Claude Code auto-discovers components in default locations and derives the plugin name from the directory name.

### 3. hooks.json Format

Located at `hooks/hooks.json` in the plugin root.

```json
{
  "description": "Optional description of hooks",
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Write|Edit",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/format-code.sh",
            "timeout": 30,
            "async": false,
            "statusMessage": "Formatting..."
          }
        ]
      }
    ],
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Bash",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/security-check.sh"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

**All supported event types**: `SessionStart`, `SessionEnd`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `PostToolUseFailure`, `PermissionRequest`, `PermissionDenied`, `Stop`, `StopFailure`, `SubagentStart`, `SubagentStop`, `TaskCreated`, `TaskCompleted`, `TeammateIdle`, `InstructionsLoaded`, `ConfigChange`, `CwdChanged`, `FileChanged`, `WorktreeCreate`, `WorktreeRemove`, `PreCompact`, `PostCompact`, `Elicitation`, `ElicitationResult`, `Notification`

**Hook handler types**:
- `command`: Shell command execution. Fields: `command` (required), `async`, `shell`, `timeout`, `if`, `statusMessage`, `once`
- `http`: POST to a URL. Fields: `url` (required), `headers`, `allowedEnvVars`, `timeout`
- `prompt`: LLM evaluation. Fields: `prompt` (required), `model`, `timeout`
- `agent`: Agentic verifier with tools. Fields: `prompt` (required), `timeout`

**Matcher syntax**: Omitted or `"*"` matches all. Pipe-separated strings for exact match (e.g., `"Write|Edit"`). Other patterns treated as JavaScript regex.

**Environment variables available**: `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` (plugin install dir) and `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}` (persistent data dir).

### 4. Agent Definition Files

Located in `agents/` directory. Each agent is a Markdown file with YAML frontmatter.

```markdown
---
name: security-reviewer
description: Reviews code for security vulnerabilities. Use when analyzing code for security issues.
model: sonnet
effort: medium
maxTurns: 20
disallowedTools: Write, Edit
---

You are a security expert. When invoked, analyze code for:
1. SQL injection vulnerabilities
2. XSS attack vectors
3. Authentication bypasses
4. Insecure data handling
```

**Supported frontmatter fields for plugin agents**:

| Field | Required | Description |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| `name` | Yes | Unique identifier, lowercase with hyphens |
| `description` | Yes | When Claude should delegate to this agent |
| `model` | No | `sonnet`, `opus`, `haiku`, full model ID, or `inherit` |
| `effort` | No | `low`, `medium`, `high`, `max` |
| `maxTurns` | No | Maximum agentic turns |
| `tools` | No | Allowlist of tools |
| `disallowedTools` | No | Tools to deny |
| `skills` | No | Skills to preload at startup |
| `memory` | No | `user`, `project`, or `local` |
| `background` | No | `true` to always run as background task |
| `isolation` | No | Only valid value: `"worktree"` |
| `color` | No | Display color: red/blue/green/yellow/purple/orange/pink/cyan |

**Security restriction for plugin agents**: `hooks`, `mcpServers`, and `permissionMode` fields are **NOT supported** in plugin-shipped agents and are silently ignored.

Located at `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` in the marketplace repository root.

      "keywords": ["formatting", "prettier"],

      "strict": true
    },
    {

        "source": "github",
        "repo": "company/deploy-plugin",
        "ref": "v2.0.0",
        "sha": "a1b2c3d4e5f6..."
      },
      "description": "Deployment automation"
    }
  ]
}
```

**Required marketplace fields**:

| Field | Type | Description |
|-------|------|-------------|
| `name` | string | Kebab-case identifier. Users see this in install commands. |
| `owner` | object | `name` (required string), `email` (optional string) |
| `plugins` | array | List of plugin entries |

**Reserved marketplace names** (cannot be used): `claude-code-marketplace`, `claude-code-plugins`, `claude-plugins-official`, `anthropic-marketplace`, `anthropic-plugins`, `agent-skills`, `knowledge-work-plugins`, `life-sciences`. Names impersonating official marketplaces are also blocked.

**Optional metadata**: `metadata.description`, `metadata.version`, `metadata.pluginRoot` (base directory prepended to relative source paths).

**Plugin entry required fields**: `name` (string) and `source` (string or object).

**Plugin source types**:
- **Relative path**: `"./plugins/my-plugin"` (string starting with `./`)
- **GitHub**: `{ "source": "github", "repo": "owner/repo", "ref": "v2.0", "sha": "abc123..." }`
- **Git URL**: `{ "source": "url", "url": "https://...", "ref": "...", "sha": "..." }`
- **Git subdirectory**: `{ "source": "git-subdir", "url": "...", "path": "...", "ref": "...", "sha": "..." }`

```yaml

---

- **Missing** — feature or behavior not implemented at all
- **Incorrect** — implemented but wrong
- **Incomplete** — partially implemented, gaps remain
- **Untested** — implemented but no test coverage

## Reporting Format

For each finding report:
1. File and line number (or "N/A — not implemented")
2. Category (missing, incorrect, incomplete, untested)
3. What the spec requires (quote or reference the spec)
4. What the implementation does (or doesn't do)
5. Severity: critical / high / medium / low

If you notice issues outside the scoped files, list them separately under "Out-of-scope observations" at the end.

Be thorough within scope. Cross-reference every spec requirement.
When done, send your complete findings to the team lead.
If you find ZERO in-scope issues, say so explicitly.

=== agent-teams-simplify-and-harden ===
---
name: agent-teams-simplify-and-harden
description: "Implementation + audit loop using parallel agent teams with structured simplify, harden, and document passes. Spawns implementation agents to do the work, then audit agents to find complexity, security gaps, and spec deviations, then loops until code compiles cleanly, all tests pass, and auditors find zero issues or the loop cap is reached. Use when: implementing features from a spec or plan, hardening existing code, fixing a batch of issues, or any multi-file task that benefits from a build-verify-fix cycle."
---

# Agent Teams Simplify & Harden

A two-phase team loop that produces production-quality code: **implement**, then **audit using simplify + harden passes**, then **fix audit findings**, then **re-audit**, repeating until the codebase is solid or the loop cap is reached.

## When to Use

- Implementing multiple features from a spec or plan
- Hardening a codebase after a batch of changes
- Fixing a list of issues or gaps identified in a review
- Any task touching 5+ files where quality gates matter

## Pipeline Integration

This skill replaces stages 2–4 of the standard pipeline (execution, review, learning) with a team-based loop. It can follow `plan-interview` or run standalone — every upstream artifact is optional.


=== context-surfing ===
---
name: context-surfing
description: >
  Monitors context window health throughout a session and rides peak context quality for maximum output fidelity.
  Activates automatically after plan-interview and intent-framed-agent. Stays active through execution and hands off
  cleanly to simplify-and-harden and self-improvement when the wave completes naturally or exits via handoff.
  Use this skill whenever a multi-step agent task is underway and session continuity or context drift is a concern.
  Especially important for long-running tasks, complex refactors, or any work where degraded context would silently
  corrupt the output. Trigger even if the user doesn't say "context surfing" — if an agent task is running across
  multiple steps with intent and a plan already established, this skill is live.
---

# Context Surfing

The agent rides the wave of peak context. When the wave crests, it commits. When it detects drift, it pulls out cleanly — saving state, handing off, and letting the next session catch the next wave.

No wipeouts. No zombie sessions. Only intentional, high-fidelity execution.

---


=== intent-framed-agent ===
---
name: intent-framed-agent
description: "Frames coding-agent work sessions with explicit intent capture and drift monitoring. Use when a session transitions from planning/Q&A to implementation for coding tasks, refactors, feature builds, bug fixes, or other multi-step execution where scope drift is a risk."
---

# Intent Framed Agent

## Purpose

This skill turns implicit intent into an explicit, trackable artifact at the
moment execution starts. It creates a lightweight intent contract, watches for
scope drift while work is in progress, and closes each intent with a short
resolution record.

## Scope (Important)

Use this skill for coding tasks only. It is designed for implementation work
that changes executable code.

Do not use it for general-agent activities such as:

=== plan-interview ===
---
name: plan-interview
description: |
  Ensures alignment between user and Claude during feature/spec planning through a structured interview process.

  Use this skill when the user invokes /plan-interview before implementing a new feature, refactoring, or any non-trivial implementation task. The skill runs an upfront interview to gather requirements across technical constraints, scope boundaries, risk tolerance, and success criteria before any codebase exploration.

  Do NOT use this skill for: pure research/exploration tasks, simple bug fixes, or when the user just wants standard planning without the interview process.
---

# Plan Interview Skill

## Purpose

Run a structured requirements interview before planning implementation. This ensures alignment between you and the user by gathering explicit requirements rather than making assumptions.

## When Invoked

User calls `/plan-interview <task description>`.


=== self-improvement ===
---
name: self-improvement
description: "Captures learnings, errors, and corrections to enable continuous improvement. Use when: (1) A command or operation fails unexpectedly, (2) User corrects Claude ('No, that's wrong...', 'Actually...'), (3) User requests a capability that doesn't exist, (4) An external API or tool fails, (5) Claude realizes its knowledge is outdated or incorrect, (6) A better approach is discovered for a recurring task. Also review learnings before major tasks. For CI-only/headless learning capture, use self-improvement-ci."
---

# Self-Improvement Skill

Log learnings and errors to markdown files for continuous improvement. Coding agents can later process these into fixes, and important learnings get promoted to project memory.

## Quick Reference

| Situation | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| Command/operation fails | Log to `.learnings/ERRORS.md` |
| User corrects you | Log to `.learnings/LEARNINGS.md` with category `correction` |

| API/external tool fails | Log to `.learnings/ERRORS.md` with integration details |
| Knowledge was outdated | Log to `.learnings/LEARNINGS.md` with category `knowledge_gap` |
| Found better approach | Log to `.learnings/LEARNINGS.md` with category `best_practice` |
| Simplify/Harden recurring patterns | Log/update `.learnings/LEARNINGS.md` with `Source: simplify-and-harden` and a stable `Pattern-Key` |

460	  budget:
461	    max_diff_ratio: 0.2        # Max additional changes as ratio of original diff
462	    max_time_seconds: 60       # Hard time limit
463	  simplify:
464	    enabled: true
465	    auto_apply_cosmetic: true  # Cosmetic fixes applied without prompting
466	    refactor_requires_approval: true  # ALWAYS true -- cannot be disabled
467	  harden:
468	    enabled: true
469	    auto_apply_patches: true   # Simple security patches applied without prompting
470	    refactor_requires_approval: true  # ALWAYS true -- cannot be disabled
471	  document:
472	    enabled: true
473	    max_comments: 5
474	  stop_hook:
475	    mode: "interactive"
476	    show_diff_preview: true
477	    allow_skip_all: true
478	    timeout_seconds: 300       # 5 min -- human is at the keyboard
479	    timeout_action: "flag"     # Assume they stepped away, don't discard
480	  skip_patterns:               # Glob patterns to exclude from review
481	    - "**/*.test.*"
482	    - "**/*.spec.*"
483	    - "**/migrations/**"
484	```
485	
486	## Design Decisions
487	
488	**Why post-completion and not continuous?**
489	Continuous review during implementation creates feedback loops that slow the agent down and can cause oscillation (simplify, then re-complicate, then re-simplify). Post-completion gives the agent a stable codebase to review against.
490	
491	**Why simplify-first, not refactor-first?**
492	Agents love to refactor. Given permission to "improve" code, they will restructure it. But most post-task improvements are cosmetic: a dead import, a bad name, a needlessly deep conditional. These account for 80%+ of the value with near-zero risk. Refactoring carries real risk -- it can introduce bugs, break tests, and bloat diffs. By making simplification the default and refactoring the exception, the skill delivers consistent value without surprise rewrites. The bar for a refactor should be "this is genuinely wrong" not "this could be slightly better."
493	
494	**Why a budget?**
495	Without constraints, agents will use review passes as license for unbounded refactoring. The 20% rule keeps the skill focused: improve what you built, don't rebuild it.
496	
497	**Why separate simplify from harden?**
498	They require different mindsets. Simplify asks "is this the clearest expression of my intent?" while Harden asks "how could this be exploited?" Conflating them leads to mediocre results on both. Running them sequentially also lets us prioritize security fixes when budget is tight.
499	
500	**Why the document micro-pass?**
501	Agents are terrible at documenting their reasoning unprompted. Humans reviewing agent-generated code consistently report that the biggest friction is understanding *why* a choice was made. Five comments is a trivial cost for enormous review-time savings.
502	
503	## Future Considerations
504	
505	- **Team calibration**: Allow teams to weight the review checklist (e.g., "we care more about injection vectors than naming")
506	- **Diff-aware context loading**: For large codebases, intelligently load only the files and symbols relevant to the diff rather than the full project
507	- **Cross-skill composition**: Simplify & Harden could feed into a "PR Description" skill that uses its summary to auto-generate meaningful PR descriptions

budget:
    max_diff_ratio: 0.2        # Max additional changes as ratio of original diff
    max_time_seconds: 60       # Hard time limit
  simplify:
    enabled: true
    auto_apply_cosmetic: true  # Cosmetic fixes applied without prompting
    refactor_requires_approval: true  # ALWAYS true -- cannot be disabled
  harden:
    enabled: true
    auto_apply_patches: true   # Simple security patches applied without prompting
    refactor_requires_approval: true  # ALWAYS true -- cannot be disabled
  document:
    enabled: true
    max_comments: 5
  stop_hook:
    mode: "interactive"
    show_diff_preview: true
    allow_skip_all: true
    timeout_seconds: 300       # 5 min -- human is at the keyboard
    timeout_action: "flag"     # Assume they stepped away, don't discard
  skip_patterns:               # Glob patterns to exclude from review
    - "**/*.test.*"
    - "**/*.spec.*"
    - "**/migrations/**"
```

## Design Decisions

**Why post-completion and not continuous?**
Continuous review during implementation creates feedback loops that slow the agent down and can cause oscillation (simplify, then re-complicate, then re-simplify). Post-completion gives the agent a stable codebase to review against.

**Why simplify-first, not refactor-first?**
Agents love to refactor. Given permission to "improve" code, they will restructure it. But most post-task improvements are cosmetic: a dead import, a bad name, a needlessly deep conditional. These account for 80%+ of the value with near-zero risk. Refactoring carries real risk -- it can introduce bugs, break tests, and bloat diffs. By making simplification the default and refactoring the exception, the skill delivers consistent value without surprise rewrites. The bar for a refactor should be "this is genuinely wrong" not "this could be slightly better."

**Why a budget?**
Without constraints, agents will use review passes as license for unbounded refactoring. The 20% rule keeps the skill focused: improve what you built, don't rebuild it.

**Why separate simplify from harden?**
They require different mindsets. Simplify asks "is this the clearest expression of my intent?" while Harden asks "how could this be exploited?" Conflating them leads to mediocre results on both. Running them sequentially also lets us prioritize security fixes when budget is tight.

**Why the document micro-pass?**
Agents are terrible at documenting their reasoning unprompted. Humans reviewing agent-generated code consistently report that the biggest friction is understanding *why* a choice was made. Five comments is a trivial cost for enormous review-time savings.

## Future Considerations

- **Team calibration**: Allow teams to weight the review checklist (e.g., "we care more about injection vectors than naming")
- **Diff-aware context loading**: For large codebases, intelligently load only the files and symbols relevant to the diff rather than the full project
- **Cross-skill composition**: Simplify & Harden could feed into a "PR Description" skill that uses its summary to auto-generate meaningful PR descriptions

# pskoett-ai-skills

A collection of skills for AI agents. Follows the [Agent Skills specification](https://agentskills.io/specification).
This repository is my personal skill testing ground.

## Philosophy

Every skill in this collection is built around a philosophy — a principle that addresses a specific failure mode in how agents work today. `plan-interview` is about collaborative planning: before codebase exploration starts, user and agent run a structured interview to align on constraints, scope, risk, and success criteria — and to surface whether a preparatory refactor should come before the main change. `intent-framed-agent` makes execution intent explicit so scope drift becomes visible. `context-surfing` monitors context quality and exits cleanly before degradation corrupts output. `simplify-and-harden` uses the peak context at end-of-task for a focused quality and security review. `self-improvement` turns repeated mistakes into durable rules that persist across sessions.

The common thread: agents have peak context at specific moments — after planning, mid-execution, at completion, after learning — and these skills are designed to exploit those peaks. Each skill encodes a philosophy that agents struggle to internalize on their own, turning it into a structured workflow they can follow reliably. `skill-pipeline` ties these pieces together by classifying the task and routing it through the right depth of process.

## Install

```bash
npx skills add pskoett/pskoett-ai-skills
```

## Structure

```
skills/
  skill-name/
    SKILL.md         # Required - skill definition with YAML frontmatter
    scripts/         # Optional - executable code
    references/      # Optional - documentation loaded on demand
    assets/          # Optional - templates, images, data files
```

## Skills

| Skill | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| [agent-teams-simplify-and-harden](skills/agent-teams-simplify-and-harden/) | Implementation + audit loop using parallel agent teams with structured simplify, harden, and document passes |
| [context-surfing](skills/context-surfing/) | Monitors context window health and rides peak context quality for maximum output fidelity during multi-step execution |
| [dx-data-navigator](skills/dx-data-navigator/) | Query DX Data Cloud for developer productivity metrics, DORA metrics, PR/deployment data, and engineering analytics |
| [intent-framed-agent](skills/intent-framed-agent/) | Captures a lightweight intent contract at execution start and monitors coding-task drift until resolution |
| [plan-interview](skills/plan-interview/) | Runs a structured interview before planning non-trivial implementations |
| [self-improvement](skills/self-improvement/) | Captures learnings and errors with hook-based activation and automatic skill extraction |
| [skill-pipeline](skills/skill-pipeline/) | Pipeline orchestrator that classifies tasks and routes them through the right skill combination at the right depth |
| [simplify-and-harden](skills/simplify-and-harden/) | Post-completion self-review that runs simplify, harden, and micro-documentation passes before signaling done |

## Experimental (CI Skills)

These skills are experimental and currently part of the testing ground setup.

| Skill | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| [self-improvement-ci](skills/self-improvement-ci/) | CI-only self-improvement workflow for recurring failure-pattern capture using gh-aw |
| [simplify-and-harden-ci](skills/simplify-and-harden-ci/) | CI-only simplify/harden workflow for pull requests using gh-aw with headless scan/report gates |

## Skill Pipeline

Each skill prevents a distinct failure mode:

| Skill | Failure it prevents |
|-------|-------------------|
| `plan-interview` | Building the wrong thing |
| `intent-framed-agent` | Scope creep during execution |
| `context-surfing` | Degraded-context corruption |
| `simplify-and-harden` | Shipping rough/insecure code |
| `self-improvement` | Repeating the same mistakes |

### Lifecycle

```
[plan-interview] → [intent-framed-agent] ⟂ [context-surfing] → [simplify-and-harden] → [self-improvement]
                                          ↑   concurrent    ↑
```

**Stage 1 — Planning** (manual gate): `plan-interview` runs a structured interview and produces a plan file in `docs/plans/`. This is the only skill that requires explicit invocation (`/plan-interview`). Downstream skills activate automatically when present, but each works independently if earlier stages are skipped.

**Stage 2 — Execution** (concurrent monitoring): `intent-framed-agent` captures the intent frame and monitors *scope* drift. `context-surfing` monitors *context quality* drift. Both run simultaneously. If both fire at once, context-surfing's exit takes precedence — degraded context makes scope checks unreliable.

**Stage 3 — Review** (post-completion): `simplify-and-harden` runs three passes (simplify, harden, document) on the completed work.

**Stage 4 — Learning** (automatic): `self-improvement` captures recurring patterns from the session and promotes them to project-level instruction files.

### Artifacts at each stage

| Stage | Artifact | Location |
|-------|----------|----------|
| Planning | Plan file | `docs/plans/plan-NNN-<slug>.md` |
| Execution | Intent frame | Emitted in session output |
| Execution | Handoff file (on drift exit) | `.context-surfing/handoff-<slug>-<timestamp>.md` |
| Review | Structured YAML summary | Appended to task output |
| Learning | Learning entries | `.learnings/LEARNINGS.md`, `ERRORS.md`, `FEATURE_REQUESTS.md` |

### Pipeline depth

Every skill works standalone. The pipeline is the recommended combination, not a hard dependency — each skill silently adapts when upstream artifacts are absent.

Match depth to complexity:

| Task | Skills |
|------|--------|
| Trivial (typo fix, rename) | None |
| Small (isolated bug fix) | `simplify-and-harden` |
| Medium (feature, multi-file) | `intent-framed-agent` + `simplify-and-harden` |
| Large (refactor, new architecture) | Full pipeline |
| Long-running (multi-session) | Full pipeline — `context-surfing` is critical |

## Usage

To use a skill, add it to your agent's configuration or reference it directly.

### Hook Setup

Several skills support automatic activation via hooks. Add to `.claude/settings.json`:

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "UserPromptSubmit": [{
      "matcher": "",
      "hooks": [
        {
          "type": "command",
          "command": "./skills/self-improvement/scripts/activator.sh"
        },
        {
          "type": "command",
          "command": "./skills/context-surfing/scripts/handoff-checker.sh"
        }
      ]
    }]
  }
}
```

| Hook Script | Skill | Purpose |
|-------------|-------|---------|
| `self-improvement/scripts/activator.sh` | self-improvement | Reminds to evaluate learnings after tasks |
| `context-surfing/scripts/handoff-checker.sh` | context-surfing | Detects unread handoff files from previous context exits |

Both hooks are lightweight (~50-100 tokens) and skip silently when not applicable.

## Contributing

Feel free to submit PRs with new skills or improvements to existing ones.

1	# Hook Setup Guide
2	
3	Configure automatic self-improvement triggers for AI coding agents.
4	
5	## Overview
6	
7	Hooks enable proactive learning capture by injecting reminders at key moments:
8	- **UserPromptSubmit**: Reminder after each prompt to evaluate learnings
9	- **PostToolUse (Bash)**: Error detection when commands fail
10	
11	## Claude Code Setup
12	
13	### Option 1: Project-Level Configuration
14	
15	Create `.claude/settings.json` in your project root:
16	
17	```json
18	{
19	  "hooks": {
20	    "UserPromptSubmit": [
21	      {
22	        "matcher": "",
23	        "hooks": [
24	          {
25	            "type": "command",
26	            "command": "./skills/self-improvement/scripts/activator.sh"
27	          }
28	        ]
29	      }
30	    ],
31	    "PostToolUse": [
32	      {
33	        "matcher": "Bash",
34	        "hooks": [
35	          {
36	            "type": "command",
37	            "command": "./skills/self-improvement/scripts/error-detector.sh"
38	          }
39	        ]
40	      }
41	    ]
42	  }
43	}
44	```
45	
46	### Option 2: User-Level Configuration
47	
48	Add to `~/.claude/settings.json` for global activation:
49	
50	```json
51	{
52	  "hooks": {
53	    "UserPromptSubmit": [
54	      {
55	        "matcher": "",
56	        "hooks": [
57	          {
58	            "type": "command",
59	            "command": "~/.claude/skills/self-improvement/scripts/activator.sh"
60	          }
61	        ]
62	      }
63	    ]
64	  }
65	}
66	```
67	
68	### Minimal Setup (Activator Only)
69	
70	For lower overhead, use only the UserPromptSubmit hook:
71	
72	```json
73	{
74	  "hooks": {
75	    "UserPromptSubmit": [
76	      {
77	        "matcher": "",
78	        "hooks": [
79	          {
80	            "type": "command",
81	            "command": "./skills/self-improvement/scripts/activator.sh"
82	          }
83	        ]
84	      }
85	    ]
86	  }
87	}
88	```
89	
90	## Codex CLI Setup
91	
92	Codex uses the same hook system as Claude Code. Create `.codex/settings.json`:
93	
94	```json
95	{
96	  "hooks": {
97	    "UserPromptSubmit": [
98	      {
99	        "matcher": "",
100	        "hooks": [
101	          {
102	            "type": "command",
103	            "command": "./skills/self-improvement/scripts/activator.sh"
104	          }
105	        ]
106	      }
107	    ]
108	  }
109	}
110	```
111	
112	## GitHub Copilot Setup
113	
114	Copilot doesn't support hooks directly. Instead, add guidance to `.github/copilot-instructions.md`:
115	
116	```markdown
117	## Self-Improvement
118	
119	After completing tasks that involved:
120	- Debugging non-obvious issues
121	- Discovering workarounds
122	- Learning project-specific patterns
123	- Resolving unexpected errors
124	
125	Consider logging the learning to `.learnings/` using the format from the self-improvement skill.
126	
127	For high-value learnings that would benefit other sessions, consider skill extraction.
128	```
129	
130	## Verification
131	
132	### Test Activator Hook
133	
134	1. Enable the hook configuration
135	2. Start a new Claude Code session
136	3. Send any prompt
137	4. Verify you see `<self-improvement-reminder>` in the context
138	
139	### Test Error Detector Hook
140	
141	1. Enable PostToolUse hook for Bash
142	2. Run a command that fails: `ls /nonexistent/path`
143	3. Verify you see `<error-detected>` reminder
144	
145	### Dry Run Extract Script
146	
147	```bash
148	./skills/self-improvement/scripts/extract-skill.sh test-skill --dry-run
149	```
150	
151	Expected output shows the skill scaffold that would be created.
152	
153	## Troubleshooting
154	
155	### Hook Not Triggering
156	
157	1. **Check script permissions**: `chmod +x scripts/*.sh`
158	2. **Verify path**: Use absolute paths or paths relative to project root
159	3. **Check settings location**: Project vs user-level settings
160	4. **Restart session**: Hooks are loaded at session start
161	
162	### Permission Denied
163	
164	```bash
165	chmod +x ./skills/self-improvement/scripts/activator.sh
166	chmod +x ./skills/self-improvement/scripts/error-detector.sh
167	chmod +x ./skills/self-improvement/scripts/extract-skill.sh
168	```
169	
170	### Script Not Found
171	
172	If using relative paths, ensure you're in the correct directory or use absolute paths:
173	
174	```json
175	{
176	  "command": "/absolute/path/to/skills/self-improvement/scripts/activator.sh"
177	}
178	```
179	
180	### Too Much Overhead
181	
182	If the activator feels intrusive:
183	
184	1. **Use minimal setup**: Only UserPromptSubmit, skip PostToolUse
185	2. **Add matcher filter**: Only trigger for certain prompts:
186	
187	```json
188	{
189	  "matcher": "fix|debug|error|issue",
190	  "hooks": [...]
191	}
192	```
193	
194	## Hook Output Budget
195	
196	The activator is designed to be lightweight:
197	- **Target**: ~50-100 tokens per activation
198	- **Content**: Structured reminder, not verbose instructions
199	- **Format**: XML tags for easy parsing
200	
201	If you need to reduce overhead further, you can edit `activator.sh` to output less text.
202	
203	## Security Considerations
204	
205	- Hook scripts run with the same permissions as Claude Code
206	- Scripts only output text; they don't modify files or run commands
207	- Error detector reads `CLAUDE_TOOL_OUTPUT` environment variable
208	- All scripts are opt-in (you must configure them explicitly)
209	
210	## Disabling Hooks
211	
212	To temporarily disable without removing configuration:
213	
214	1. **Comment out in settings**:
215	```json
216	{
217	  "hooks": {
218	    // "UserPromptSubmit": [...]
219	  }
220	}
221	```
222	
223	2. **Or delete the settings file**: Hooks won't run without configuration

### Extraction Detection Triggers

Watch for these signals that a learning should become a skill:

**In conversation:**
- "Save this as a skill"
- "I keep running into this"
- "This would be useful for other projects"
- "Remember this pattern"

**In learning entries:**
- Multiple `See Also` links (recurring issue)
- High priority + resolved status
- Category: `best_practice` with broad applicability
- User feedback praising the solution

### Skill Quality Gates

Before extraction, verify:

- [ ] Solution is tested and working
- [ ] Description is clear without original context
- [ ] Code examples are self-contained
- [ ] No project-specific hardcoded values
- [ ] Follows skill naming conventions (lowercase, hyphens)

## Multi-Agent Support

This skill works across different AI coding agents with agent-specific activation.

### Claude Code

**Activation**: Hooks (UserPromptSubmit, PostToolUse)
**Setup**: `.claude/settings.json` with hook configuration
**Detection**: Automatic via hook scripts

### Codex CLI

**Activation**: Hooks (same pattern as Claude Code)
**Setup**: `.codex/settings.json` with hook configuration
**Detection**: Automatic via hook scripts

### GitHub Copilot

**Activation**: Manual (no hook support)
**Setup**: Add to `.github/copilot-instructions.md`:

```markdown
## Self-Improvement

After solving non-obvious issues, consider logging to `.learnings/`:
1. Use format from self-improvement skill
2. Link related entries with See Also
3. Promote high-value learnings to skills

Ask in chat: "Should I log this as a learning?"
```

**Detection**: Manual review at session end

### Agent-Agnostic Guidance

Regardless of agent, apply self-improvement when you:

1. **Discover something non-obvious** - solution wasn't immediate
2. **Correct yourself** - initial approach was wrong
3. **Learn project conventions** - discovered undocumented patterns
4. **Hit unexpected errors** - especially if diagnosis was difficult
5. **Find better approaches** - improved on your original solution

### Copilot Chat Integration

For Copilot users, add this to your prompts when relevant:

> After completing this task, evaluate if any learnings should be logged to `.learnings/` using the self-improvement skill format.

Or use quick prompts:
- "Log this to learnings"
- "Create a skill from this solution"
- "Check .learnings/ for related issues"

485	
486	## Design Decisions
487	
488	**Why post-completion and not continuous?**
489	Continuous review during implementation creates feedback loops that slow the agent down and can cause oscillation (simplify, then re-complicate, then re-simplify). Post-completion gives the agent a stable codebase to review against.
490	
491	**Why simplify-first, not refactor-first?**
492	Agents love to refactor. Given permission to "improve" code, they will restructure it. But most post-task improvements are cosmetic: a dead import, a bad name, a needlessly deep conditional. These account for 80%+ of the value with near-zero risk. Refactoring carries real risk -- it can introduce bugs, break tests, and bloat diffs. By making simplification the default and refactoring the exception, the skill delivers consistent value without surprise rewrites. The bar for a refactor should be "this is genuinely wrong" not "this could be slightly better."
493	
494	**Why a budget?**
495	Without constraints, agents will use review passes as license for unbounded refactoring. The 20% rule keeps the skill focused: improve what you built, don't rebuild it.
496	
497	**Why separate simplify from harden?**
498	They require different mindsets. Simplify asks "is this the clearest expression of my intent?" while Harden asks "how could this be exploited?" Conflating them leads to mediocre results on both. Running them sequentially also lets us prioritize security fixes when budget is tight.
499	
500	**Why the document micro-pass?**
501	Agents are terrible at documenting their reasoning unprompted. Humans reviewing agent-generated code consistently report that the biggest friction is understanding *why* a choice was made. Five comments is a trivial cost for enormous review-time savings.
502	
503	## Future Considerations
504	
505	- **Team calibration**: Allow teams to weight the review checklist (e.g., "we care more about injection vectors than naming")
506	- **Diff-aware context loading**: For large codebases, intelligently load only the files and symbols relevant to the diff rather than the full project
507	- **Cross-skill composition**: Simplify & Harden could feed into a "PR Description" skill that uses its summary to auto-generate meaningful PR descriptions
508

## Design Decisions

**Why post-completion and not continuous?**
Continuous review during implementation creates feedback loops that slow the agent down and can cause oscillation (simplify, then re-complicate, then re-simplify). Post-completion gives the agent a stable codebase to review against.

**Why simplify-first, not refactor-first?**
Agents love to refactor. Given permission to "improve" code, they will restructure it. But most post-task improvements are cosmetic: a dead import, a bad name, a needlessly deep conditional. These account for 80%+ of the value with near-zero risk. Refactoring carries real risk -- it can introduce bugs, break tests, and bloat diffs. By making simplification the default and refactoring the exception, the skill delivers consistent value without surprise rewrites. The bar for a refactor should be "this is genuinely wrong" not "this could be slightly better."

**Why a budget?**
Without constraints, agents will use review passes as license for unbounded refactoring. The 20% rule keeps the skill focused: improve what you built, don't rebuild it.

**Why separate simplify from harden?**
They require different mindsets. Simplify asks "is this the clearest expression of my intent?" while Harden asks "how could this be exploited?" Conflating them leads to mediocre results on both. Running them sequentially also lets us prioritize security fixes when budget is tight.

**Why the document micro-pass?**
Agents are terrible at documenting their reasoning unprompted. Humans reviewing agent-generated code consistently report that the biggest friction is understanding *why* a choice was made. Five comments is a trivial cost for enormous review-time savings.

## Future Considerations

- **Team calibration**: Allow teams to weight the review checklist (e.g., "we care more about injection vectors than naming")
- **Diff-aware context loading**: For large codebases, intelligently load only the files and symbols relevant to the diff rather than the full project
- **Cross-skill composition**: Simplify & Harden could feed into a "PR Description" skill that uses its summary to auto-generate meaningful PR descriptions

By making simplification the default and refactoring the exception, the skill delivers consistent value without surprise rewrites. The bar for a refactor should be "this is genuinely wrong" not "this could be slightly better."

**Why a budget?**
Without constraints, agents will use review passes as license for unbounded refactoring. The 20% rule keeps the skill focused: improve what you built, don't rebuild it.

**Why separate simplify from harden?**
They require different mindsets. Simplify asks "is this the clearest expression of my intent?" while Harden asks "how could this be exploited?" Conflating them leads to mediocre results on both. Running them sequentially also lets us prioritize security fixes when budget is tight.

**Why the document micro-pass?**
Agents are terrible at documenting their reasoning unprompted. Humans reviewing agent-generated code consistently report that the biggest friction is understanding *why* a choice was made. Five comments is a trivial cost for enormous review-time savings.

# Multi-Agent Support

This skill works across different AI coding agents with agent-specific activation.

## Claude Code

**Activation**: Hooks (UserPromptSubmit, PostToolUse)
**Setup**: `.claude/settings.json` with hook configuration
**Detection**: Automatic via hook scripts

## Codex CLI

**Activation**: Hooks (same pattern as Claude Code)
**Setup**: `.codex/settings.json` with hook configuration
**Detection**: Automatic via hook scripts

## GitHub Copilot

**Activation**: Manual (no hook support)
**Setup**: Add to `.github/copilot-instructions.md`:

```markdown
## Self-Improvement

After solving non-obvious issues, consider logging to `.learnings/`:
1. Use format from self-improvement skill
2. Link related entries with See Also
3. Promote high-value learnings to skills

Ask in chat: "Should I log this as a learning?"
```

**Detection**: Manual review at session end

## Agent-Agnostic Guidance

Regardless of agent, apply self-improvement when you:

1. **Discover something non-obvious** - solution wasn't immediate
2. **Correct yourself** - initial approach was wrong
3. **Learn project conventions** - discovered undocumented patterns
4. **Hit unexpected errors** - especially if diagnosis was difficult
5. **Find better approaches** - improved on your original solution

## Copilot Chat Integration

For Copilot users, add this to your prompts when relevant:

> After completing this task, evaluate if any learnings should be logged to `.learnings/` using the self-improvement skill format.

Or use quick prompts:
- "Log this to learnings"
- "Create a skill from this solution"
- "Check .learnings/ for related issues"

message.content:
ultrathink do an analysis here what we need to get the full loop in our skills to start improving the complete flow Two Loops You Need to Know
Peter Skøtt Pedersen
Peter Skøtt Pedersen
People - AI - Software


April 8, 2026
If you want to improve agent output over time, you need to run two loops not one.

The inner loop happens during a running session. The agent detects a problem, checks its work, and tries to recover without you touching anything.

The outer loop happens across sessions. You capture where the agent failed, figure out what knowledge was missing, and encode it somewhere the agent can reach next time. 

Both loops are required. The inner loop catches failures in the moment. The outer loop ensures the same failures stop happening. Without both, you are not improving the system, you are just managing it.

A compact way to think about it:

Inner loop: detect, verify, recover
Outer loop: inspect, encode, regress-test

Thorsten Ball has a useful framing for why agents fail in the first place: the knowledge required to complete a task has to live somewhere. It usually lives in one of three places:

Your prompt/spec. What you explicitly tell the agent.
The codebase or harness. Types, tests, tools, conventions, documentation anything the agent can read and reason from.
Training data. What the model already knows from the world.

If the knowledge exists in at least one of those places, the agent usually has a path forward. If it doesn't exist in any of them, there's a gap. The agent will plough through anyway and fill the gap with something: infer, improvise, guess. Sometimes that works. Often it doesn't.

In workflows, the failure is often not the model. It's the assumption that the knowledge was somewhere it wasn't.

This gets more dangerous as you move to end-to-end autonomous workflows. One gap mid-run and the whole thing goes sideways, silently. You can catch some of this with CI pipelines or quality gates, and you should. But gates only cover what you thought to test for. The gaps that slip through are the ones nobody anticipated.

The two loops are how you close those gaps systematically, over time.

The Inner Loop, the agent checks itself
The inner loop is the one you can see. The agent runs, hits a problem, and adapts during execution without you touching anything. That might mean self-correcting on a bad output, but it also means replanning when a step fails, switching tools when the first approach doesn't work, handling uncertainty, or stopping instead of guessing when something critical is missing.

An agent that can do any of these mid-task operates at a fundamentally different level than one that just barrels forward.

The quality of the inner loop depends almost entirely on whether the agent has usable feedback signals: test runners, linters, Chrome DevTools CLI, API response validators. Anything that produces a clear signal the agent can read and act on. The agent doesn't need you to tell it the output was wrong if a test can. The more the agent can check itself, the fewer gaps slip through undetected.

But the inner loop has a ceiling. It can only fix what the agent can observe in the moment, with the context and tools it has at the time. It catches syntax errors and misses intent drift. It repairs a broken command and still misunderstands the actual goal.

Which is exactly why you need the second loop.

The outer loop, closing the gaps systematically
The outer loop operates across working sessions. Its job is to take what the inner loop couldn't fix and turn it into permanent harness improvements.

Its raw material is session traces full captures of what the agent did, decided, and where it went wrong. Without traces, teams iterate on memory. They patch around the last failure and rediscover the same issue two weeks later.

On a regular cadence, you have an agent read those traces and surface issues. Not you scrolling through logs an agent doing the analysis pass, finding the patterns, flagging where knowledge was missing.

Then you close the gaps:

Update instructions tighten what was ambiguous, add context that was missing
Update tools add capabilities the agent improvised around, remove tools that created confusion
Update skills refine the reusable behavior definitions the agent draws on
Create a new skill if the same gap keeps appearing with no existing coverage, that's a skill specification waiting to be written
Retest run the exact same case and verify the fix holds
Make it an eval permanently lock the case so it never silently regresses

That last step is where the discipline breaks down. Fix the issue once, move on, and it will come back. If a failure taught you something important, it should become a permanent test case. Otherwise the knowledge is still fragile.

You can't front-load the simplification. The real gaps only surface after the agent has run the task. The outer loop's job is to learn where the failure came from, then fix the right thing.

Not every failure is a knowledge gap. Some are reasoning failures. Some are poor tool strategy. Some come from an ambiguous prompt that creates bad incentives. Tracing which kind you're dealing with matters, because the fix is different each time.

Agent Skill files, MCP tool descriptions, agent context files these aren't just documentation. They are the answer to "where is the knowledge?" They are how you move knowledge from nowhere into the prompt, the codebase, or the harness, where the agent can actually reach it.

This compounds
Every outer loop improvement feeds directly back into the inner loop.

Better agent skills mean the agent has sharper behavior to draw on mid-task. Better context means fewer dead ends. Better tools mean fewer cases where the agent has to improvise around a gap. Better evals mean regressions get caught before they corrupt the next session.

The inner loop gets stronger because the harness it runs on got stronger. The knowledge gaps get smaller with every cycle. That's not linear improvement. That's compounding and it's the only sustainable way to make agentic workflows genuinely reliable over time.

In practice this could look like
Inner loop: The agent runs with access to verification tools: test output, lint results, type errors, API contract checks. When something fails, it captures what went wrong and attempts recovery before moving on. When recovery works, nothing happens from the outside. When it doesn't, the trace has the evidence.

Outer loop: Sessions are wrapped with intent capture at the start and drift detection throughout. Traces accumulate. On cadence, an agent reads them, surfaces patterns, and flags where knowledge was missing. Gaps become updated instructions, new skills, or permanent evals. The harness evolves.

The knowledge gaps close. The harness gets better. Even when the model changes, the harness determines whether those gains compound or disappear.

That's the whole game.

The model is not the moat, everyone has that its everything around it
Once you think this way, "where is the knowledge?" becomes a design constraint. Two loops become the operating model for improving agent reliability over time.

If your harness is well designed, stronger models become upside, not a migration crisis. A better model should improve your output without forcing you to rewrite your skills, restructure your context, or rediscover your process from scratch. If it does, that's the signal your design is sound.

The intelligence isn't trapped inside one model choice. It lives in the framing, the tools, the context, and the evals around it.

That's the moat.

Hat tip to Thorsten Ball's framing on knowledge location: Joy & Curiosity #80

Now I have all the files. Let me analyze each one systematically against the detect-verify-recover inner loop:

## Analysis Report: Inner Loop Coverage (Detect-Verify-Recover)

### 1. **intent-framed-agent** — SKILL.md

**What it covers:**

- **Detect:** Explicitly detects scope drift via Intent Checks. When work appears to move outside stated outcome, it captures the drift signal before escalating. Drift examples listed: "work outside stated scope", "approach changes with no explicit pivot", "new features/refactors outside constraints", "solving a different problem than stated outcome".

- **Verify (partial):** Verifies against the stated intent frame. When drift is detected, it asks: "Is this a deliberate pivot or accidental scope creep?" — this is a verification question, but it stops there. User confirms yes/no on the pivot.

**What it explicitly does NOT do:**

- Does NOT verify correct execution quality or context health. It only checks scope against the stated outcome, not whether the work is being done well.
- Does NOT attempt recovery/correction. When drift is detected and user confirms it's accidental, the instruction is simply "return to the original scope" — no active re-anchoring or recovery protocol.
- Does NOT verify completion — has no assertion that the code is correct, secure, or follows conventions. Resolution captures "Fulfilled / Partially fulfilled / Pivoted / Abandoned" but does NOT validate that fulfilled work actually meets quality gates.
- Does NOT provide feedback mechanisms to improve detection rules. Drift patterns can be "logged to self-improvement as learnings if they recur" but this is optional ("can be") not systematic.

---

### 2. **context-surfing** — SKILL.md

**What it covers:**

- **Detect (extensive):** Detects context degradation via strong and weak signals. Strong signals: "The agent contradicts a decision it already made", "A detail appears that was never in context (hallucination)", "re-opens a scope question that was explicitly resolved", "Output starts re-explaining the task rather than executing". Weak signals: "responses getting longer without getting more useful", "hedging language increases", "switches approaches mid-task without direction", "references to intent become vague", "asks clarifying question it should know".

- **Verify (extensive):** Recovery Protocol Step 1 is mandatory re-reading: "re-read whatever wave anchor artifacts are available" (intent frame, plan file, Entire CLI logs, original task). Step 2 reconciles current work against what artifacts say should be happening. Explicitly states "re-anchor reads from them directly, never from reconstructed memory".

- **Recover (extensive):** Full Recovery Protocol defined. If weak signals accumulate, pause and re-read (Step 1). Reconcile against anchor (Step 2). If it reconciles: resume. If uncertainty remains: escalate to user. If user re-grounds: integrate and resume. If user can't resolve or intent fundamentally changed: exit with handoff.

**What it explicitly does NOT do:**

- Does NOT modify code or fix bugs during recovery. Recovery is purely context re-anchoring — if context re-anchors successfully, work resumes unchanged.
- Does NOT generate new tasks or guide implementation changes. It monitors quality drift but doesn't prescribe fixes to implementation.
- Does NOT feed detected drift patterns into learning/rules. It notes drift happened, but "drift patterns observed during the session can be logged as learnings if they recur" is optional.
- Does NOT provide continuity between sessions except via handoff file. The next session must re-run plan-interview to replan.
- Does NOT verify that handoff was actually read by the next session — the hook reminds them, but doesn't gate execution.

---

### 3. **simplify-and-harden** — SKILL.md

**What it covers:**

- **Detect (extensive):** Fresh-eyes review of modified code. Simplify pass detects: dead code, naming issues, control flow problems, over-exposed APIs, over-abstraction. Harden pass detects: input validation gaps, error handling gaps, injection vectors, auth issues, secrets exposure, data exposure, dependency risk, race conditions. Spec auditor variant (referenced) detects: missing features, incorrect behavior, incomplete implementation.

- **Verify (moderate, through refactor approval):** For cosmetic fixes and patches, the agent verifies these are safe via implicit rules. For refactors and security refactors, the agent MUST describe and get explicit human approval before applying. The refactor stop hook pauses execution and asks: "Is this genuinely necessary or the benefit substantial?" — verification happens via human gate.

- **Recover (implicit):** When findings are applied, the code is modified but there is NO re-verification pass. The skill does not run tests, compile checks, or re-audit after fixes. The output notes what was applied, but does not verify the fixes work.

**What it explicitly does NOT do:**

- Does NOT feed findings back into itself or the harness in any automated way. Findings are reported in structured YAML output but no loop re-runs simplify-and-harden to check if the fixes introduced new issues.
- Does NOT update or modify `.claude.md`, `AGENTS.md`, or system prompt files. Learning candidates are emitted for `self-improvement` to handle, not acted on by this skill.
- Does NOT run compile/test verification after applying fixes. The skill is agnostic to whether the modified code actually compiles or tests pass.
- Does NOT verify findings against external sources. All detections are self-review only; no cross-check with linting tools, security scanners, or type checkers.
- Does NOT gate task completion. If a human rejects a refactor proposal, the skill continues; rejected findings still appear in output but don't block completion.

---

### 4. **agent-teams-simplify-and-harden** — SKILL.md

**What it covers:**

- **Detect (systematic):** Three specialist auditors run in parallel. Simplify-auditor detects: dead code, naming, control flow, API surface, over-abstraction, consolidation. Harden-auditor detects: input validation, error handling, injection vectors, auth/authz, secrets, data exposure, dependency risk, race conditions. Spec-auditor detects: missing features, incorrect behavior, incomplete implementation, contract violations, test coverage gaps. Multiple rounds of auditing.

- **Verify (moderate, through compilation + testing + human refactor gate):** After implementation phase: "Run compile/type checks to verify clean build. Run tests to verify all pass." Before spawning auditors. After audit finds refactors: "Evaluate whether the refactor is genuinely necessary — bar: 'Would a senior engineer say the current state is clearly wrong?'" Human gate on refactors. Between audit rounds: "Run compile + test verification" before re-auditing. Drift check before next audit round: "re-read the intent frame and plan/task breakdown. Compare the current state of the work against the original scope."

- **Recover (systematic loop):** If auditors find critical/high/medium findings, create tasks, spawn implementation agents to fix them, wait for fixes, re-run compile + tests, then spawn FRESH audit agents again. Loop up to 3 rounds maximum. If only low findings remain: "fix them inline and skip re-auditing". Exit conditions: clean audit (zero findings), low-only round, or loop cap reached.

**What it explicitly does NOT do:**

- Does NOT guarantee that audit findings are actually fixed. It creates tasks and spawns agents, but if an agent doesn't complete the task (e.g., runs out of context), the loop cap still stops. Unresolved findings are logged but execution doesn't block.
- Does NOT run independent verification of auditor findings. The auditors are read-only Explore agents, but there is no separate verification step to confirm their findings are accurate before tasks are created.
- Does NOT verify that fixes don't introduce new issues beyond what the next round of auditing catches. If fix round 1 introduces a subtle bug that auditor round 2 misses, it stays in the code.
- Does NOT feed audit findings directly into learning/rules. Like simplify-and-harden, candidates are emitted for `self-improvement` but the skill doesn't update CLAUDE.md or agent instructions.
- Does NOT prevent re-auditing the same findings across rounds. If auditor round 1 and round 2 both find the same issue (e.g., a particular input validation gap), it's flagged twice; there's no deduplication mechanism.

---

### 5. **error-detector.sh** — self-improvement hook

**What it covers:**

- **Detect:** Scans tool output (`CLAUDE_TOOL_OUTPUT` env var) for error patterns: "error:", "failed", "command not found", "No such file", "Permission denied", "fatal:", "Exception", "Traceback", "npm ERR!", "ModuleNotFoundError", "SyntaxError", "TypeError", "exit code", "non-zero". If any pattern matches, outputs a reminder.

**What it explicitly does NOT do:**

- Does NOT verify the error or categorize severity. Simple string matching only.
- Does NOT log the error automatically. Outputs a reminder suggesting to log IF the error "was unexpected", "required investigation", "might recur", "solution could benefit future sessions" — but the human must decide.
- Does NOT recover or fix the error. It only reminds; all action is manual.
- Does NOT feed back into error detection across sessions. Each error is standalone.
- Does NOT distinguish between transient errors (network blip) and systemic errors (logic bug). All matching patterns are treated equally.

---

### 6. **handoff-checker.sh** — context-surfing hook

**What it covers:**

- **Detect:** Scans for unread handoff files in `.context-surfing/` directory at session start. If found, outputs a reminder with count and file list.

- **Verify (implicit):** The reminder instructs: "Before starting new work, you MUST: Read the handoff file(s) completely" — verification that handoff was read is the human's responsibility.

**What it explicitly does NOT do:**

- Does NOT verify that the handoff is actually read. It finds the files and reminds; it doesn't gate execution or check if contents were consumed.
- Does NOT automatically load or parse the handoff. Output is human-readable only; no machine parsing.
- Does NOT verify that the next session follows the recommended re-entry point. Handoff says "pick up from X", but there is no enforcement that the session does.
- Does NOT detect if a new session ignores the handoff and starts fresh anyway. It reminds once; if the user deletes the reminder and starts new work, there is no second gate.
- Does NOT verify that the previous session's work was actually complete or that the handoff is accurate. It trusts the handoff file without validation.

---

## Summary Table

| Skill | Detect | Verify | Recover | Notes |
|-------|--------|--------|---------|-------|
| **intent-framed-agent** | Scope drift vs stated intent | User confirms pivot vs creep | Only "return to scope" — no active recovery | No quality gates, no code verification |
| **context-surfing** | Context degradation (signals + re-read) | Re-anchor against artifacts | Full recovery protocol + clean handoff exit | No code modification, no cross-session continuity guarantee |
| **simplify-and-harden** | Quality/security gaps (self-review) | Human gate on refactors | Apply fixes but don't verify (no test/compile check) | No systematic learning feedback, isolated runs |
| **agent-teams-simplify-and-harden** | Quality/security/spec gaps (auditors) | Compile + tests + human refactor gate | Loop up to 3 rounds, fresh auditors each | No verification that fixes work, dedup across rounds |
| **error-detector.sh** | Command errors (pattern match) | None | None | Passive reminder only, human decides action |
| **handoff-checker.sh** | Unread handoff files | Human reads | None | Reminder only, no gate or enforcement |

The inner loop **is distributed across skills** — no single skill covers all of detect-verify-recover. **context-surfing** has the most complete cycle (detect degradation, verify by re-anchoring, recover with handoff), but only for context quality, not code quality. **agent-teams-simplify-and-harden** has the tightest loop for code quality (detect via auditors, verify via tests + human gate, recover via fixes + re-audit), but with open gaps (unverified auditor findings, no dedup, no guarantee fixes are applied).
